title: “LET HER BREASTS SATISFY YOU”: The Marriage Advice Christians Rarely Quote From Proverbs
paragraphs:
“LET HER BREASTS SATISFY YOU”: The Marriage Advice Christians Rarely Quote From Proverbs
We warn Christians about sexual sin. But what if Scripture’s answer to lust was never merely “stop desiring”—but learn where desire becomes holy?
There is a sentence in the Bible that would probably make some Christians uncomfortable if the pastor read it slowly on Sunday morning.
“Let her breasts satisfy you at all times.”

The book we quote to our children about wisdom, discipline, laziness, anger, money, pride, and guarding the heart suddenly speaks with an intimacy many Christian conversations about marriage barely know how to handle.
And perhaps our discomfort reveals something.
Because God did not blush when He inspired Scripture to speak about marital desire.

שָׁדֶיהָ יְרַוֻּךָ בְכָל־עֵת
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
A close rendering of the thought is:
“May her breasts satisfy you at all times; may you continually be captivated by her love.”
The Hebrew word translated “breasts” is שָׁדֶיהָ — shadeha, literally “her breasts.” Scripture is not hiding behind a vague euphemism here.
But neither is Scripture being crude.
Because Proverbs 5 is not pornography wearing religious clothing.
It is wisdom defending a covenant.
And if you isolate verse 19 because it sounds provocative, you can completely miss what God is saying.
“Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well.”
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
And immediately afterward comes the warning:
Why become captivated by another woman?
The entire passage is constructed around a contrast.
Some Christians were raised with an unspoken theology that almost sounded like this:
and somehow at the altar all those years of shame are supposed to disappear before the honeymoon.
But Scripture tells a richer story.
The problem was never that husbands and wives could deeply desire one another.
The shocking message of Proverbs 5 is not merely:
Do not stop delighting in your spouse.
That is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because marriages rarely collapse in one dramatic moment.
One more morning leaving without affection.
One more anniversary treated like another date on the calendar.
One more rejection that is never discussed.
“I don't know what happened to us.”
But maybe something had been happening for years.
The person who once made your heart race became familiar.
The person you once couldn't stop talking to became the person you barely talk to.
The hand you once reached for instinctively became a hand you stopped noticing.
And somewhere between bills, children, exhaustion, disappointment, responsibilities, wounds, aging, arguments, careers, phones, ministries, and ordinary life...
That is precisely why the wording of Proverbs is so beautiful.
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say she will remain physically twenty-two forever.
Yet Scripture points the husband back toward the woman of his covenant and essentially says:
There is something breathtakingly countercultural about that.
Our world trains people to consume novelty.
Pornography teaches the eyes to wander without responsibility.
Lust wants someone's body without carrying someone's burdens.
I have heard the things you were afraid to tell anyone else.
I know the years have changed both of us.
That is far more intimate than lust.
Lust says, “What can your body do for me?”
Love asks, “How can I cherish the whole person God entrusted to me?”
And this is essential: Proverbs 5 must never be twisted into permission for sexual entitlement.
A wife's body is not her husband's property to exploit.
A husband's body is not his wife's instrument to control.

Biblical marital intimacy cannot be separated from the wider Christian commands to love sacrificially, honor one another, reject harshness, practice faithfulness, and imitate the self-giving love of Christ.
Jesus does not teach husbands to dominate their wives.
The New Testament gives husbands a far more frightening command:
Love your wife as Christ loved the church.
That turns Christian marriage upside down.
The question is no longer merely:
“Am I loving this person in a way that looks like Jesus?”
Because the deepest biblical picture of marriage eventually leads us beyond the bedroom.
Ephesians 5 reaches all the way back to Genesis—“the two shall become one flesh”—and then Paul says something astonishing:
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
Your spouse cannot save your soul.
But Christian marriage can become a living signpost pointing toward covenant faithfulness.
A bridegroom who does not abandon His bride.
A Savior who remains faithful when His people have been unfaithful.
And suddenly Proverbs 5 becomes even heavier.
Because sexual sin is never merely about bodies.
What are you asking to satisfy you?
Where are your eyes going when nobody is watching?
What secret world have you constructed behind your spouse's back?
What conversation would terrify you if your husband or wife saw it tonight?
What browser history do you keep deleting?
Whose profile do you repeatedly visit?
Whose attention have you begun craving?
What fantasy have you renamed “harmless” because admitting what it is would require repentance?
But Proverbs 5 does not end with human secrecy.
Just after warning against forbidden intimacy, Scripture says that a person's ways are before the eyes of the LORD.
That means there is no private room where God disappears.
Because the God who sees the hidden thing is also the God who can heal the hidden thing.
Maybe this article found you after failure.
Maybe pornography has hollowed out part of your marriage.
Maybe you became emotionally attached to someone who wasn't your spouse.
Maybe your spouse discovered something you thought would remain buried forever.
And now whenever you read passages about sexual purity, you don't feel conviction first.
“This is for marriages that aren't broken like mine.”
“This is for somebody other than me.”
The Bible that says flee sexual immorality is the same Bible that announces forgiveness to repentant sinners.
Jesus did not come for people who could manufacture spotless histories.
That does not make betrayal small.
Grace never needs to pretend sin wasn't devastating.
Repentance means bringing darkness into the light, abandoning excuses, telling truth, accepting consequences, seeking accountability, and walking a different road.
Forgiveness is not permission to continue secretly destroying people.
“It mattered so much that Christ carried sin to the cross.”
There is a difference between remorse because you were exposed and repentance because you finally agree with God.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to come home.
Because you can repair date nights and still have an unrepentant heart.
You can improve communication and still worship yourself.
You can delete an app and still hunger for the same darkness.
Christian transformation goes deeper than behavior management.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people receive trophies.
It is that guilty people can receive mercy because the innocent Son of God took the judgment sinners deserved.
At the cross, sin is not minimized.
It is exposed in all its horror.
And grace is revealed in all its glory.
And the person who turns to Him in repentance and faith does not have to spend eternity pretending the past never happened.
Jesus can write a future that sin did not deserve.
Not by rewriting God's definition of sin.
Maybe your marriage needs that kind of rewriting.
Maybe tonight does not need to begin with sex.
Maybe it needs to begin with honesty.
Sometimes restoration begins when somebody finally stops defending themselves.

And if your marriage has experienced serious betrayal, coercion, abuse, or danger, restoration should never mean pretending everything is fine or remaining unsafe. Seek wise pastoral help and appropriately qualified professional support. Biblical forgiveness does not require enabling abuse or eliminating necessary boundaries and consequences.
But for the husband who simply stopped noticing his wife...
For the wife who has allowed years of hurt to become silent contempt...
Bring the wound into honest conversation.
For the couple living more like roommates than lovers...
Remember the first time you realized this person mattered differently.
Remember the prayers you prayed together.
Remember what God carried you through.
And perhaps hear Proverbs again—not as embarrassment, but as wisdom.
within the tenderness, mutuality, safety, and faithfulness of marriage...
God is not embarrassed by marital intimacy.
He designed covenant before pornography corrupted desire.
He created bodies before advertisers learned to sell them.
He created marriage before culture learned to cheapen it.
Christian holiness therefore is not the extermination of desire.
It is desire brought under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody desperately needed tonight.
You do not need another secret.
You do not need another fantasy.
You do not need another stranger's attention.
You need to remember the sacred weight of covenant.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only believer fighting for purity, healing, and faithfulness.
And don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it doesn't.

But if this truth can strengthen a marriage, expose a hidden compromise, confront pornography, encourage repentance, or lead one wounded person toward Jesus, sharing it can become a simple act of Christian witness.
Send it privately to the couple fighting for their marriage.

Financial support is not a condition of glorifying God, salvation, spiritual maturity, or God's blessing. But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one voluntary way believers participate in helping biblical teaching reach more people.
Invite the Christian whose marriage is quietly bleeding.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing intelligent or beautiful to say about desire.
Share what may help somebody else.
But never confuse the resource with the Source.
A stronger marriage cannot save you.
And perhaps that is ultimately what Proverbs 5 has been whispering beneath all its surprisingly intimate language.
And when sin has already shattered what you thought could never be repaired...
come back to the Savior whose specialty has always been resurrection.
Because sometimes the most scandalous thing about your story isn't what you did in the darkness.
It's what Jesus can still make beautiful after you finally bring it into the light.
